# Part A: notes from the browser

Fill in the table as you work through Part A on the course page. Replace each
`...` with your answer. (This is plain Markdown: no R needed.)

| Gene | UniProt accession | Location in UniProt | Main location in HPA | HPA reliability |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CANX | P27824 | ER membrane, single-pass type I | Endoplasmic reticulum | Enhanced |
| TOMM20 | Q15388 | Mitochondrion outer membrane, single-pass | Mitochondria | Enhanced |
| GOLGA2 | Q08379 | cis-Golgi network membrane (peripheral, cytoplasmic side) | Golgi apparatus | Enhanced |
| LMNB1 | P20700 | Nucleus lamina | Nuclear membrane | Supported |
| CAT | P04040 | Peroxisome matrix | Vesicles | Supported |
| LAMP1 | P11279 | Lysosome membrane (also late endosome, cell membrane) | no IF data | none |

**INS in the HPA single-cell section:** cell type enriched, pancreatic islet cells
(about 86 000 nCPM); essentially absent from all other cell types.

**HeLa (CVCL_0030) in Cellosaurus:** species *Homo sapiens*, disease
HPV-related endocervical adenocarcinoma, virus HPV18; "the most frequent contributor
to cell lines contamination" (e.g. HEp-2, CVCL_1906, is a HeLa derivative).

(Answers checked 2026-11-18: UniProt 2026_04, HPA 26.0.)

# Part B: protein sizes from UniProt

## The proteins

Thirteen human proteins: the organelle markers from Part A, plus a few famous
proteins from the lectures. The compartment is where each protein mainly works.

```{r proteins}
markers <- data.frame(
  accession = c("P27824", "Q15388", "P11279", "Q08379", "P20700", "P04040",
                "P05023", "P13569", "P60709", "P07437", "Q8WZ42", "P62805",
                "P04406"),
  label = c("Calnexin (CANX)", "TOM20 (TOMM20)", "LAMP1", "GM130 (GOLGA2)",
            "Lamin B1 (LMNB1)", "Catalase (CAT)", "Na/K pump (ATP1A1)",
            "CFTR", "Actin (ACTB)", "Tubulin beta (TUBB)", "Titin (TTN)",
            "Histone H4", "GAPDH"),
  compartment = c("ER", "Mitochondrion", "Lysosome", "Golgi", "Nucleus",
                  "Peroxisome", "Plasma membrane", "Plasma membrane",
                  "Cytoskeleton", "Cytoskeleton", "Cytoskeleton", "Nucleus",
                  "Cytosol")
)
markers
```

## Fetch the data (your chunk 1)

Build the UniProt address as a character string called `uniprot_url`, then read
it into a data frame called `proteins` with `read.delim(uniprot_url)`. The course
page (step B2) gives the three pieces of the address.

```{r uniprot-fetch, eval = !use_snapshot}
base <- "https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/accessions?accessions="
ids <- paste(markers$accession, collapse = ",")
fields <- "&fields=accession,gene_primary,protein_name,length,mass&format=tsv"
uniprot_url <- paste0(base, ids, fields)
proteins <- read.delim(uniprot_url)
head(proteins)
```

The next chunk is given. It saves a dated copy of what UniProt returned (or reads
the course snapshot), notes the UniProt release, and adds a column with the mass
in kDa.

```{r uniprot-record}
data_source <- "not fetched yet"
uniprot_release <- "unknown"
retrieved <- "not yet"

if (use_snapshot) {
  snapshot_file <- "data/uniprot-proteins-2026-11-18.csv"
  if (!file.exists(snapshot_file)) {
    snapshot_file <- paste0("https://henriksson-lab.github.io/course_cellbiology/",
                            "bioinfo-protein-atlas/data/uniprot-proteins-2026-11-18.csv")
  }
  proteins <- read.csv(snapshot_file)
  data_source <- paste("course snapshot", snapshot_file)
  uniprot_release <- "2026_04"
  retrieved <- "2026-11-18"
} else if (exists("proteins")) {
  dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)
  write.csv(proteins, file.path("data", paste0("uniprot-proteins-", Sys.Date(), ".csv")),
            row.names = FALSE)
  data_source <- uniprot_url
  headers <- curlGetHeaders(uniprot_url)
  uniprot_release <- trimws(sub(".*: ", "",
    grep("^x-uniprot-release:", headers, ignore.case = TRUE, value = TRUE)))
  retrieved <- as.character(Sys.Date())
}

proteins <- merge(markers, proteins, by.x = "accession", by.y = "Entry")
proteins$mass_kda <- proteins$Mass / 1000
proteins[, c("label", "compartment", "Length", "mass_kda")]
```

## Largest and smallest (your chunk 2)

Find the largest and the smallest protein in `proteins` (by mass), and how many
times heavier the largest is. Store them as `largest`, `smallest` and `ratio`.
Hint: `which.max()` and `which.min()`.

```{r largest-smallest}
largest <- proteins[which.max(proteins$Mass), ]
smallest <- proteins[which.min(proteins$Mass), ]
ratio <- largest$Mass / smallest$Mass
largest[, c("label", "Length", "mass_kda")]
smallest[, c("label", "Length", "mass_kda")]
ratio
```

## Plot (your chunk 3)

Make a dot plot with `ggplot2`: protein mass (kDa) on a **logarithmic** x axis,
one row per protein, coloured by compartment. Give the axis a label with its unit
and add a caption naming the data source.

```{r mass-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
ggplot(proteins, aes(x = mass_kda, y = reorder(label, mass_kda), colour = compartment)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Protein mass (kDa, log scale)", y = NULL, colour = "Compartment",
       caption = paste0("Data: UniProtKB release ", uniprot_release,
                        ", retrieved ", retrieved)) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## What the plot shows

Write two or three sentences here. Use inline R for at least one number (for
example the ratio), so the text updates by itself if the data change.

The largest protein, `r largest$label`, is `r format(round(largest$mass_kda), big.mark = " ")` kDa
(`r format(largest$Length, big.mark = " ")` amino acids); the smallest,
`r smallest$label`, is `r round(smallest$mass_kda, 1)` kDa. Titin is about
`r round(ratio)` times heavier, and most proteins lie between 30 and 170 kDa, so on
a linear axis all of them except titin would be squeezed into the left edge. On a
log axis each step is a factor of 10, and every protein gets room.
